note_tweet.text:
A US court has defended academic freedom:

A US judge has dismissed a defamation lawsuit against scientific publisher Elsevier. The allegations were raised by the company Global Plasma Solutions which produces an air purifier. They were annoyed that Elsevier published a paper by researchers at the Illinois Institute of Technology who questioned whether the technology does what the company promises. They had tested one of the company’s devices and reported in 2021 that it did little to remove airborne particles. The company alleged that the researchers concealed contradictory data and that Elsevier published the paper despite a failed peer review. 

On 22 October, a judge in North Carolina rejected the lawsuit. He judged there was insufficient evidence that Elsevier knowingly published false information or recklessly disregarded whether it was true, as would have been required for the defamation claim. 

This lawsuit is not an isolated case. I have personally known scientists who were sued by companies for inconvenient findings. Most of the lawsuits were unsuccessful. However, I am afraid that the threat of being sued alone deters some scientists from investigating the claims of companies. I previously talked about this here:

https://t.co/l4djzrLzGo

More details about the lawsuit here: https://t.co/VmbWbnpzpg

Economic worries typically dominate midterm elections, and 2026 is no different. The affordability question, which directly ties to the economy and direction of the country, appears to be the core issue driving voter sentiment.

What is notable this year is how 4 foreign policy issues have affected those economic issues. CFR experts break down how the Iran war, U.S. trade policy, AI, and immigration could be shaping voters’ perceptions of the economy and the United States’ role in the world.

Among voters, there is a “lack of enthusiasm about continuing involvement in Middle East wars,” said CFR expert Elliott Abrams. They sense that foreign wars divert resources from domestic needs and, more importantly, have started to feel a “direct and immediate” economic effect, Abrams added.

A CFR poll authored by CFR's Allison Smith found that Americans understood tariffs to raise prices of not only goods but also services. Smith said that this could have an effect on voter sentiment. “Consumers are definitely making the connection between tariffs and the higher prices that they’re paying,” she said.

CFR expert Pierre Yared pointed to the COVID-19 pandemic and the U.S. housing shortage as true drivers of the affordability crisis. “Voters’ concerns come from the sticker shock from the cumulative inflation they experienced after the pandemic, which is still around since the price level has not come back down,” Yared said.

Immigration and immigration policy remain important issues in the 2026 midterms. “I don’t think that American voters were prepared for what the Trump administration has delivered, and I think that’s what you’re seeing in the polls now,” Edward Alden, a CFR senior fellow specializing in immigration policy, said. American voters want a sense that the U.S. government is maintaining control over immigration, he added.

Voter mood around AI heading into the midterms is “more anxious than enthusiastic,” CFR technology and national security expert Jessica Brandt said. The adoption of AI tools has increased the share of Americans who fear that the technology could cause their jobs to become obsolete, and public polling indicates that voters are connecting data center buildouts nationwide to rising electricity bills.

Over the last 20 years, China has emerged as the United States and Europe’s most important foreign source of upstream inputs of critical medicines. China has also surged up the innovation ladder, becoming a preferred setting for critical first-in-human drug trials and for developing and manufacturing promising new medicines.

“Essential medicines are a dangerous chokepoint because when China dominates their supply chain, therapeutic substitutes will not be readily available if those supplies are withheld—and China has already proven it is willing to weaponize the pharmaceutical supply chain against other nations,” write expert @TomBollyky and Elena Every in a new report.

"The gradual loss of transatlantic pharmaceutical capacity to China is not simply the result of market conditions or a rapacious industry but the product of decades of coordinated Chinese state intervention. Reversing that loss will require an equal, coordinated, and sustained U.S. and EU response," they write.

“The United States and the European Union need to overcome the tension in their transatlantic partnership, particularly on drug pricing. President Donald Trump has broken new ground, using trade tools to lower prescription drug prices at home by seeking to raise them abroad, especially in Europe, and to return drug manufacturing to the United States."

“The answer to reducing pharmaceutical supply chain dependence on China is targeted, meaningful transatlantic cooperation that maximizes the advantages of both the United States and the European Union—not resorting to uncoordinated protectionism, loosely defined partnerships, or squabbles over domestic drug pricing policies,” they argue.

note_tweet.text:
Under pressure from Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Trump administration may be within days of launching a nuclear strike on Iran. The target would be Pickax Mountain in central Iran, where Israeli intelligence claims the Iranian government has restarted its nuclear enrichment program. No conventional weapon in the American arsenal can penetrate 300 feet of solid granite to destroy the tunnels where enrichment is supposedly taking place. The only military option is a nuclear strike. Netanyahu has been pushing hard for one. “Bibi calls Trump about it every day,” says an informed observer.

Netanyahu is cornered and desperate. After last week’s election results, he can’t form a government unless Trump intervenes directly in Israeli politics and brokers a deal with other parties that gives Netanyahu 61 seats in the Knesset. Otherwise, he is out as prime minister and on his way to ignominy, investigations and possibly jail. Netanyahu must stay close to Trump. He needs this war.

To that end, he’s applied maximum pressure to his closest allies in the administration, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and CENTCOM commander Brad Cooper. Both oppose a negotiated settlement to the war they’ve so grievously mismanaged; both are pushing to restart major combat operations. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and CIA director John Ratcliffe are also following Netanyahu’s lead, as are leaders of the Democratic Party. In a recent meeting on the subject, former president Barack Obama said he opposes the current Iran peace deal being drafted in Doha.

The rest of America’s longtime allies in the Middle East are terrified by the prospect of more war. On September 27th, Netanyahu flew secretly to Abu Dhabi to enlist the UAE in his lobbying effort for a final attack on Iran. The Emiratis refused. After eight months of conflict, Gulf economies are teetering. So are global energy and fertilizer markets. They won’t recover soon. Globally, there are a total of about 850 supertankers used to transport oil from producers to the rest of the world. In October alone, 11 of them were badly damaged in Hormuz. At this pace, a global depression is imminent. A nuclear strike would radically accelerate the destruction. Fallout from a ground explosion at Pickax Mountain would contaminate the Persian Gulf, poisoning the water supply for 100 million people.

And those are just some of the immediate consequences for the region. The rest of the world is every bit as exposed. No country other than the United States has ever used a nuclear weapon in war. Some would like to. An American nuclear attack on Iran would set a new precedent. The Russians have already told at least two other governments that an American nuclear strike on Iran would free them to use nuclear weapons against Ukraine. Pakistan and India would be tempted to do the same against each other, as would North Korea against Seoul. After the first nuclear strike, World War Three is inevitable. That war would be short and final.

We’ve been sleepwalking toward this moment for months. Since February, the administration has quietly rewritten America’s nuclear doctrine to make first use of so-called “battlefield nukes” easier and therefore more likely. No one in Washington in either party seems bothered by this. Now we’re on the brink of it.

Close observers say Trump is likely to decide by next weekend whether or not to use nuclear weapons. That would be November 7, six days from now. To his credit, he’s hesitating. At the moment, Trump is listening to his vice president, JD Vance, and to his envoy and friend Steve Witkoff, both of whom argue a deal with Iran can be made.

They’re right, though it won’t be simple. The Iranians are famously frustrating to negotiate with under any circumstances, and elements of that government have become more radical since Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and his family were killed in February. After decades of isolation, even relatively moderate Iranian leaders seem confused by how decisions are made in the West. (There is a widespread belief in Tehran, for example, that the United States government controls Israel.) But overall, people who have spoken to decision-makers in Iran say there is consensus there that more war is bad for everyone and a deal is worth making.

One group that hasn’t been consulted so far is the global population — the hundreds of millions of people who will be killed along with their children if Trump is pushed by Netanyahu into launching a nuclear strike next week. Now would be the time for them to speak up.
